questions.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?

options.text: The C=C double bond
options.explanation: The carbon-carbon double bond defines the alkene family and its chemistry.

options.text: The OH group
options.explanation: OH defines the alcohols, a family met later in the topic.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: That belongs to the halogenoalkanes from the previous note.

options.text: A carbon-oxygen double bond
options.explanation: No oxygen appears in the alkene functional group.

questions.stem: An alkene has n = 4. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C3H8
options.explanation: The carbon count must equal n, which is four here.

options.text: C4H8
options.explanation: Substituting into CnH2n gives eight hydrogens for four carbons, matching but-1-ene.

options.text: C4H10
options.explanation: That is the alkane count; the double bond costs two hydrogens.

options.text: C4H6
options.explanation: Two double bonds would be needed for six; an alkene carries one.

questions.stem: Why are alkenes classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons?

options.text: Because they are diluted with water in storage
options.explanation: Nothing about solutions enters the definition.

options.text: Because they cannot react with anything
options.explanation: The opposite holds: the openable bond makes them more reactive.

options.text: Because their C=C double bond can open to add more atoms
options.explanation: Spare bonding capacity at the double bond is exactly what unsaturated records.

options.text: Because they contain fewer carbon atoms than alkanes
options.explanation: Chain length is not the test; bonding capacity is.

questions.stem: What happens to the bonding at each carbon when a double bond opens?

options.text: Each carbon keeps the double bond and adds new bonds anyway
options.explanation: Opening means the double bond is gone; it cannot persist and add too.

options.text: Each carbon loses one bond entirely
options.explanation: Bonds are replaced, not destroyed; four remain at each carbon.

options.text: The carbons separate into free atoms
options.explanation: The chain stays intact; only the bond type changes.

options.text: Each carbon ends with four single bonds instead of one double and two singles
options.explanation: Opening the double bond converts the spare capacity into two new single bonds.

questions.stem: How does the reactivity of alkenes compare with alkanes, and why?

options.text: Alkenes are much more reactive because their double bond can open
options.explanation: The available bonding capacity at C=C gives alkenes routes alkanes lack.

options.text: Alkenes are less reactive because they are lighter
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant; the openable bond drives the difference.

options.text: They are equally reactive since both are hydrocarbons
options.explanation: The functional group difference is precisely why they differ.

options.text: Alkanes are more reactive because they are saturated
options.explanation: Saturation closes off reactions; unsaturation opens them.

questions.stem: Write down the general formula that every alkene obeys.
questions.modelAnswer: The alkenes follow CnH2n, two hydrogens fewer than the alkane recipe.

questions.stem: Which bond defines the functional group shared by all alkenes?
questions.modelAnswer: Every alkene carries a C=C double bond as its functional group.

questions.stem: Explain why an alkene reacts far more readily than an alkane with bromine.
questions.modelAnswer: The C=C double bond can open, letting each carbon form one more single bond with the incoming atoms, whereas an alkane's bonds are already saturated and cannot open, so the alkene is much more reactive.

questions.stem: An alkene molecule is measured to contain 6 carbon atoms. Deduce its molecular formula.
questions.modelAnswer: Substituting n = 6 into CnH2n gives C6H12.

questions.stem: Which molecular formula belongs to propene?

options.text: C4H8
options.explanation: Four carbons belongs to but-1-ene, not propene.

options.text: C3H6
options.explanation: With n = 3 the alkene recipe gives six hydrogens, and the table lists propene as C3H6.

options.text: C3H8
options.explanation: That is propane, the three-carbon alkane with no double bond.

options.text: C2H4
options.explanation: Two carbons is ethene, one rung below propene.

questions.stem: Where is the C=C bond in pent-2-ene?

options.text: Between the fourth and fifth carbon atoms
options.explanation: Counting from the nearer end would name that bond pent-1-ene as well.

options.text: Pentene has no double bond
options.explanation: Every alkene by definition carries the C=C bond.

options.text: Between the second and third carbon atoms
options.explanation: The 2 in pent-2-ene marks the first carbon of the double bond, counting from the nearer end.

options.text: Between the first and second carbon atoms
options.explanation: That position would be pent-1-ene, one number lower.

questions.stem: Why does ethene have the formula C2H4 rather than C2H6?

options.text: Ethene has lost two hydrogen atoms over time
options.explanation: Formulae are structural facts, not decay records.

options.text: Because ethene carries two oxygen atoms
options.explanation: No oxygen exists in any alkene formula.

options.text: Because ethene is an alkane in disguise
options.explanation: The double bond places it firmly in the alkene family.

options.text: The double bond uses two bonding capacities that hydrogens would otherwise fill
options.explanation: The C=C bond consumes one bond from each carbon, leaving room for two fewer hydrogens.

questions.stem: What does a displayed formula of but-1-ene show that its molecular formula C4H8 does not?

options.text: The exact position of the double bond and every single bond drawn
options.explanation: The drawing fixes the double bond location and shows all bonds, which the bare formula cannot.

options.text: The number of carbon atoms
options.explanation: The molecular formula already gives that count.

options.text: The mass of the molecule
options.explanation: Mass is calculable from the formula and never drawn.

options.text: The state of the compound at room temperature
options.explanation: Physical state is not part of any structural representation.

questions.stem: Which notation is explicitly not required for alkenes in this specification?

options.text: Drawing displayed formulae
options.explanation: Drawing up to four carbons is explicitly required.

options.text: Cis/trans or E/Z notation
options.explanation: The spec wording excludes cis/trans and E/Z labels from the requirement.

options.text: The stem-suffix naming system
options.explanation: The naming system is required and examined.

options.text: The general formula CnH2n
options.explanation: The general formula is a required know item for alkenes.

questions.stem: Give the molecular formula of the alkene but-1-ene.
Between which two carbon atoms does the double bond sit in pent-2-ene?
questions.modelAnswer: Between the second and third carbon atoms of the chain.

questions.stem: Explain why every alkene contains two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbons.
questions.modelAnswer: Two of the links a saturated chain would spend on hydrogens are taken up by the carbon-carbon double bond, so the family carries two fewer hydrogens: CnH2n instead of CnH2n+2.

questions.stem: A student draws but-1-ene with the C=C shown as a single line between the first two carbons. State which family the drawing now represents and what the correct drawing must show.
questions.modelAnswer: Drawn with one line between those carbons the picture reads as the alkane butane; the correct displayed formula must show the double bond as two parallel lines.
